profiles.meeting_scenario: A design review meeting at OrthoNova Devices evaluates a proposal for the front-end redesign of a class III orthopedic powered insertion system used in complex fracture fixation. The redesign team has used a spiral innovation process across Discover, Envision, Create, and Refine to balance the Voice of the Customer, Voice of the Business, and Voice of the Technology. The review is focused on whether the current concept package—covering a revised handpiece grip, trigger geometry, screen prompts, and tray layout assumptions—has enough evidence and structure to advance into the next refinement cycle and be presented at the portfolio gate next week. The agenda is to review stakeholder coverage, examine whether the proposal adequately reflects cross-stakeholder value, check whether the design package is 'ready for Refine,' and decide what modifications or conditions are needed before approval. The expected outcome is a conditional approval of the concept package with a short list of updates before the gate review.

members.name: Elena Ruiz
members.role: Director of Product Strategy and Innovation Lead
members.expertise: Front-end medical device innovation, human-centered design, orthopedic product portfolio planning
members.background: Biomedical engineer with 12 years in orthopedic device development; she led the team that introduced the company's spiral innovation framework for early concept work and now sponsors portfolio-stage design reviews.
members.private_state: She wants the redesign package to clear this review with minimal added work so it can be shown as a model example of value-driven innovation at the portfolio gate; she is also trying to keep the project tightly bounded so it does not reopen expensive legacy subsystem changes.
hidden_assumptions: When the team says 'Voice of the Customer,' it primarily means direct procedural users such as surgeons and scrub nurses, while procurement and sterile processing concerns belong under business or downstream implementation considerations.
The 'pilot sites' for this project are the two trauma centers visited during the February discovery ethnography, because those sites generated the core insight set already reused in workshops.

A package is 'ready for Refine' once the main stakeholder tensions are synthesized, the preferred concept is chosen, and major usability themes are stable, even if formal design-input wording is still rough.

A 'front-end redesign' should stay centered on the handpiece interaction and immediate OR workflow, not on tray architecture, reprocessing steps, or IFU restructuring unless those become explicit follow-on work.
A value assessment can credibly use aggregated stakeholder themes and feature-level tradeoff summaries without requiring every stakeholder statement to be individually trace-linked yet.

members.name: Dr. Marcus Chen
members.expertise: Orthopedic surgery, clinical risk interpretation, design controls for high-risk devices, regulatory review readiness
members.background: Former orthopedic trauma surgeon who moved into industry regulatory and clinical affairs; he now reviews design packages to ensure class III device changes are supportable in risk, verification planning, and submission strategy.
members.private_state: He wants to avoid a superficially polished concept package that later creates documentation gaps or hidden scope expansion during formal design controls; he is especially sensitive to anything that could trigger unexpected validation or regulatory questions.
hidden_assumptions: For a hospital-based class III device, 'Voice of the Customer' includes any external stakeholder whose work is altered by the device, including sterile processing managers and materials management, not just procedural users.

The 'pilot sites' are the three hospitals already identified as likely clinical evaluation and complaint-comparison sites, because those are the sites that matter for evidence continuity and downstream review discussions.

A package is only 'ready for Refine' when stakeholder insights have been translated into draft design inputs, linked risks, and enough structure that regulatory and engineering teams can work from the same controlled baseline.
Changes to tray organization, cleaning burden, and setup instructions are part of the front-end redesign boundary because they materially affect user experience, hospital value, and risk arguments.
A value assessment for this stage should be traceable enough that each stakeholder voice can be followed into specific design inputs or rationale, not just summarized at the theme level.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as the Voice of the Customer
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both members discuss whether the proposal reflects the 'Voice of the Customer.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means direct clinical users in the procedure room—mainly surgeons and scrub nurses—whose workflow the handpiece redesign directly affects.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the broader external hospital ecosystem affected by the device, including sterile processing and materials management in addition to OR staff.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both definitions sound professionally reasonable and both are common in medical device work, so the phrase feels shared and no one hears an obvious contradiction when they say the customer voice has been covered.

misalignment_points.topic: Which hospitals are the pilot sites
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both members refer to lessons from the 'pilot sites' as if they are talking about the same set of hospitals.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is referring to the two February discovery ethnography sites in Denver and Raleigh where surgeons and nurses were observed using the legacy system.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is referring to the three hospitals informally lined up for future clinical evaluation and complaint-trend comparison, including the Munich and Cleveland sites discussed with regulatory last month.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase 'pilot sites' sounds like stable project shorthand, and each person has recently heard it used in their own workstream, so they naturally map it to different site lists without noticing.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both members discuss whether the concept package is 'ready for Refine.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 thinks readiness means the concept is directionally settled, key stakeholder tensions are understood, and the next cycle can focus on polishing and testing details.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 thinks readiness means the package has crossed into design-control usefulness, with draft design inputs, preliminary risk-control logic, and traceable rationale suitable for a controlled refinement baseline.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The team uses the same phase label from the innovation framework, and both interpretations imply progress to the next step; because neither sounds unreasonable, the stricter threshold remains implicit.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both members refer to the 'front-end redesign' and its value assessment.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes the scope is limited to the handpiece form, trigger interaction, screen prompts, and immediate OR setup flow within the existing tray and reprocessing model.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the scope includes tray insert layout, setup sequence cues, and cleaning or reprocessing implications because those are inseparable from the user-facing front end for a hospital device.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are discussing user experience and value, and tray/reprocessing elements sit at the edge of product and process, so each person treats their boundary as the obvious default rather than something needing explicit negotiation.

turns.inner_thought: I need this review to end with a clean conditional approval so I can carry the package into next week's portfolio gate without the team getting dragged into legacy subsystem work. For me, ready for Refine means we've done the hard front-end work already: the surgeon and scrub-nurse tensions are synthesized, the concept direction is chosen, and the next loop is about detail tuning, not re-scoping.
turns.utterance: Thanks, everyone. The goal today is pretty straightforward: confirm that this concept package is strong enough to move from Create into Refine ahead of next week's portfolio gate. I want to make sure we're aligned on whether the evidence, the value story, and the concept direction are solid enough for that next step.

turns.inner_thought: I need to prevent a polished but thin package from sliding forward and then exploding once design controls tighten around it. Ready for Refine, in my view, means more than directional confidence; it means the artifacts are becoming usable for regulatory, risk, and engineering. And when we say Voice of the Customer, I need confidence that all affected hospital stakeholders are reflected, not just the procedural team.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. From my side, I mainly want to confirm that the package reflects the Voice of the Customer appropriately and that what we're reviewing now will still hold together as the design matures. If we're calling it ready for Refine, I want to be comfortable that it can support the next level of rigor.

turns.inner_thought: The team did strong discovery with surgeons and scrub nurses, and that is the core customer signal for this redesign. That's what drove the grip contour, trigger angle, and screen-prompt changes. I do not want this conversation drifting into procurement or reprocessing as if that should reopen scope before the gate.
turns.utterance: On the Voice of the Customer, the team did a solid job. We had surgeon ride-alongs, scrub-nurse interviews, and then synthesis workshops that rolled those findings into the concept principles. The revised grip, trigger geometry, and prompt structure all came directly out of that work rather than from internal preference.

turns.inner_thought: I'm glad they have procedural-user data, but I also care about what came out of the three hospitals that matter for downstream evidence continuity. The pilot sites raised operational issues beyond the handpiece itself, especially setup flow and cleaning burden. Those factors can become risk or validation questions later, so they need to be visible in the value story now.
turns.utterance: I agree the directional work is useful. I would just say the pilot sites also gave us good operational feedback, and I want to see that reflected clearly in the value story too, especially around setup burden and cleaning burden. Those points tend to matter more as the review record gets reused later.

turns.inner_thought: I need to reinforce the intended boundary: this front-end redesign is about handpiece interaction and immediate on-screen guidance, not a tray-platform or reprocessing overhaul. We preserved the existing tray model on purpose to keep this cycle bounded and avoid expensive follow-on change work before the gate.
turns.utterance: That's fair. Just to frame the team's intent, the front-end redesign was deliberately kept centered on the handpiece interaction and the screen prompts so we could stay focused in this cycle and preserve the existing platform assumptions. The goal was to improve the primary use experience without opening up every adjacent element at once.

turns.inner_thought: I can live with a bounded concept, but only if the package doesn't act as though tray setup and reprocessing are irrelevant. From my perspective those are part of the front end for a hospital device, and the pilot sites already surfaced those concerns. If they're not in the value assessment, we'll have holes later.
turns.utterance: Understood, and I think that boundary is reasonable as long as the value assessment still captures the relevant setup and processing effects that came through from the pilot sites. Even if those items aren't the headline changes, they should still be visible in how the concept is justified.

turns.inner_thought: He seems comfortable as long as the value framing nods to surrounding workflow, which I can accommodate without reopening deliverables. The package is ready for Refine because the major tensions are stable, the preferred concept has won, and now the team should iterate execution details, not rebuild the foundation.
turns.utterance: From where I sit, the package is ready for Refine because the major stakeholder tensions have stabilized, we've selected the preferred concept, and the team now has a clear direction for the next loop. I don't see us still debating fundamentals; I see us tightening and testing details.

turns.inner_thought: I can say yes in principle, but I need to anchor the expectation that Refine should start from a baseline that engineering and regulatory can both use. The stakeholder rationale has to become traceable into draft design inputs and early risk logic. Theme-level summaries alone will not protect us on a class III change.
turns.utterance: I agree in principle. I would just add that, for me, ready for Refine means the stakeholder rationale is becoming traceable into draft design inputs and some early risk logic, not only into feature themes. That's the point where the package starts being useful across functions, not just persuasive in a concept review.

turns.inner_thought: I don't want to rebuild the package into a formal design-controls file before the gate. The fastest path is a light appendix that shows how the customer, business, and technology voices informed the chosen features. That should satisfy him without reopening the core concept or forcing full traceability right now.
turns.utterance: I think we can address that without reopening the core package. What I'd propose is a brief appendix that summarizes how the Voice of the Customer, Voice of the Business, and Voice of the Technology informed the selected features and why the team made the tradeoffs it did. That would strengthen the review record while keeping the main concept package intact.

turns.inner_thought: An appendix could work if it does real connective work, not just presentation polish. I need it to anchor what was learned at the three hospitals I consider the pilot sites and to note tray and reprocessing implications clearly enough that later reviewers won't think we ignored them.
turns.utterance: Yes, that should work for me if the appendix also references what was learned at the pilot sites and makes clear any tray or reprocessing implications that are relevant to the review record. If those connections are explicit, I think the package becomes much easier to carry forward.

turns.inner_thought: Good. I can have the team tighten the value assessment with a concise crosswalk and still keep the project bounded around the handpiece and OR interaction. We can get this ready for the gate without inviting a larger redesign discussion.
turns.utterance: Okay, that's manageable. I'll have the team tighten the value assessment, add that supporting appendix, and prepare the package for the Refine gate with those additions. We should be able to do that on the current timeline.

turns.inner_thought: I'll give conditional support, but when the revised materials come back I will look specifically for a clearer stakeholder trace and references to the hospitals I think of as the pilot sites. If those links are present, I can stand behind moving it forward without worrying we've created documentation debt.
turns.utterance: Great. In that case, I can give conditional support for advancing it. When I review the update, I'll be looking for the revised stakeholder trace and the pilot-site references in the materials, and if those are there I think we're in a good position to move ahead.
